For example, it recovered a geometry optimization that reached its iteration limit by restarting from saved coordinates with a fresh approximate Hessian. The workflow completed in approximately 12 hours; for context, we estimate that a human researcher implementing the same workflow from scratch would require approximately one working week, including setup, troubleshooting, analysis, and reporting.

After completing the calculations, the agent assembled the results into an illustrated report supported by molecular structures, scripts, and calculation records (Fig. 15). Its analysis compared computed outcomes with initial predictions, including stronger-than-expected binding for 2-methylpyridine and distinct binding modes for 3-hydroxypyridine. This case demonstrates sustained execution of a scientist-guided computational investigation, connecting workflow implementation, job management, error recovery, and interpretation within a single research task.

Condensed Matter Physics. Sage-A1.5 performed autonomous crystal-structure refinement through iterative numerical optimization and feedback-guided parameter updates. Refinement from powder X-ray diffraction involves coupled background, lattice, and atomic parameters, requiring careful selection of which variables to update. Starting from a PXRDgen-generated Sc2​Au6\mathrm{Sc_{2}Au_{6}} structure, Sage-A1.5 coordinated three roles: a Planner selected parameter blocks, an Executor ran bounded trials using a constrained Torch-based refinement engine, and a Reviewer assessed the resulting diagnostics. An independent numerical gate checked geometric constraints and the required decrease in the weighted profile residual, RwpR_{\mathrm{wp}}, before committing an update. Each subsequent trial started from the last accepted state (Fig. 16).

Across eight trials, the workflow first stabilized scale and background, then tested cell lengths and angles before refining atomic coordinates in blocks. Cell-length refinement produced the largest decrease, 2.1215 percentage points. The third trial’s negligible angular improvement was rejected by the Reviewer; in the fifth trial, the numerical gate overrode an acceptance recommendation because RwpR_{\mathrm{wp}} had slightly increased. Six updates were accepted overall, reducing RwpR_{\mathrm{wp}} from 88.3091% to 86.1092%, an absolute decrease of 2.1999 percentage points. The substantial remaining mismatch limits conclusions about structural accuracy. Nevertheless, this case demonstrates how explicit parameter selection, diagnostic review, and independent acceptance checks can connect sequential refinement decisions to a traceable improvement in the fitting objective.

Electrochemistry. Sage-A1.5 used experimental feedback to revise mechanistic hypotheses and identify a high-yield reaction condition from historical data. The case retrospectively examines alternating-current Friedel–Crafts alkylation of 1-bromoethylbenzene using Pt–Pt electrodes, without conducting new experiments. Forty historical records defined the target reaction and an eight-variable search space: solvent, electrolyte, additive, current, frequency, reaction time, arene volume, and electrolyte loading. Categorical choices were restricted to recorded members, and continuous variables to historical ranges. A mechanistic graph informed by 16 literature sources provided candidate-ranking hypotheses. Five batches, each containing four measured conditions, supplied yield feedback for revising those hypotheses (Fig. 17).

The replay linked changes in observed rankings to specific model edits. Low-frequency observations contradicted an initially favorable high-frequency connection, prompting its removal. Later feedback motivated a reaction-time penalty for overreaction and a proposed interaction between cation residence time and solvent-mediated proton quenching. The cumulative best isolated yield across batches was 32%, 32%, 43%, 89%, and 89%. The highest recorded value, EXP-038, used dichloromethane, 1 Hz, 10 mA, 96 min, 500 μ\muL of arene, and 100 μ\muL of hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP). The model associated HFIP with cationic transition-state stabilization and reduced quenching, but the historical comparisons do not establish these effects causally. This case illustrates an interpretable feedback loop in which measured outcomes revise mechanistic working hypotheses while identifying a high-yield condition within the available historical data.

Computational Biology. Sage-A1.5 iteratively optimized a fluorescence spot detection pipeline, using evaluation feedback to refine model training and inference across diverse microscopy datasets. The task covers nine datasets spanning synthetic microscopy, fluorescence in situ hybridization, and live-cell imaging. In the recorded run, Sage-A1.5 developed a hybrid pipeline combining U-Net predictions with a Laplacian-of-Gaussian (LoG) fallback. Across eight evaluation submissions, the agent progressively revised its approach, introducing test-time augmentation, adaptive detection thresholds, and changes to the detection pipeline. Later iterations further refined normalization, background subtraction, and training objectives based on evaluation feedback (Fig. 18a). The recorded aggregate_improvement increased from −0.0469-0.0469 to 0.11580.1158, reflecting the improvements achieved through successive revisions.

A complementary visualization from a separate retained run compares predicted spots with reference annotations on the same DNA-FISH image (Fig. 18b). The overlay reveals matched detections, unmatched predictions, and missed reference spots, providing a qualitative assessment alongside the benchmark results. This case illustrates how Sage-A1.5 uses evaluation feedback to revise an image-analysis pipeline and progressively improve its detection performance.

5 Limitation and Future Work

In this report, we have developed Sage-A1.5, a 35B MoE model that shifts the focus of agent training from expanding single-task skills to composing capabilities over long horizons. Rather than relying on fixed rules in an external scaffold, we train the model to organize parallel subagents and verify intermediate evidence within its own execution policy, and then merge specialized domain teachers across search, coding, science, and real-world workflows through unified outcome–process post-training. This provides a practical route for a compact open model to tackle complex, multi-stage engineering and scientific problems.

During this effort, we also observed that organizing long-horizon work requires more than task delegation and mid-course verification. On the execution side, our current orchestration and verification training still centers on search and research synthesis, while ultra-long trajectories can still accumulate heavy context overhead; meanwhile, the unified model does not yet fully retain the peak performance of every domain teacher after joint post-training. On the application side, our scientific showcases still operate within computational simulations and historical data replays rather than active physical experiments. In future work, we will use intermediate verification points as natural boundaries to compress completed exploration history into concise stage records, extend learned orchestration to broader engineering workflows while reducing cross-domain distillation loss, and work with scientists to connect Sage-A1.5 with real-world experimental validation.
